episode_title: The Monk Who Collected 999 Swords and Died Standing: The Real Benkei
youtube_title: He Took 999 Swords and Died Standing — But the Records Barely Mention Benkei
youtube_description:
Legend says that on a June day in 1189, a giant monk stood before his master's hall at Koromogawa, pierced by arrows, and died on his feet. He is said to have taken 999 swords before a boy defeated him. Yet the Kamakura chronicle names him barely at all. Where does the real Benkei end and the legend begin? Follow time-travelling reporter Tokio Kamiya as he files a dispatch from Koromogawa, 1189.

📰 Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former Tokyo foreign correspondent. His grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to one day of Japan's past at a time. He can watch and he can speak, but he can never change what happens. Every episode is his dispatch from the scene.

🌐 Official site: https://samurai-chronicles.com

🇯🇵 A Japanese perspective on Japanese history — created by a Japanese history enthusiast.

1. McCullough, Helen Craig — "Yoshitsune: A Fifteenth-Century Japanese Chronicle" (Stanford University Press, 1966)
2. Sansom, George — "A History of Japan to 1334" (Stanford University Press, 1958)
3. Friday, Karl F. — "Samurai, Warfare and the State in Early Medieval Japan" (Routledge, 2004)
4. Mass, Jeffrey P. — "The Development of Kamakura Rule, 1180–1250: A History with Documents" (Stanford University Press, 1979)

shorts_narration: 999 swords. One bridge. One boy who beat him. A hill in 1189, and a monk who died on his feet. Or did he? This is Benkei.

scenes.narration: Let me start with what is solid, and I warn you, it is thin. The Kamakura shogunate keeps its own chronicle, the Azuma Kagami, compiled about a century later. I find it names a monk, Benkei, among the men who follow Yoshitsune when he flees Kyoto in 1185. That is nearly all. No birth date, no family, no battle in which he fights. I turn the pages of my notebook twice, in case I missed him. I think history seldom bothers to write down a bodyguard. It writes down the man he guards.

scenes.narration: Now the story, and I mark it as a story. The Gikeiki, a tale written down long after these events, says he is born in Kumano, son of the head priest of the Kumano shrines, after his mother carries him longer than any child. He is born with long hair and teeth, they say, and the village calls him a demon child. He is sent to the monastery on Mount Hiei, grows taller than every monk, and learns to read. I cannot confirm one line of it. I note it down anyway, because it is the version Japan will keep.

scenes.narration: Now the famous night, again as the story tells it. A towering monk guards a bridge in Kyoto, taking the sword of every swordsman who dares to cross. He has 999. He wants a thousand. Then a slender youth in a hooded cloak, almost a boy, steps onto the bridge, leaps along the rail, and beats him. The monk kneels. I should be honest. The earliest telling I can find sets this duel at a temple, and the bridge only arrives later. No one can show me a single sword. I think a good legend needs a number.

scenes.narration: Back to what is solid. The war between the Minamoto and the Taira is real, and it is huge. In 1184 and 1185, Yoshitsune, the younger half-brother of Yoritomo, wins at Ichi-no-tani, at Yashima, and at Dan-no-ura, where the Taira fleet goes under the waves. I read the chronicle's account of these battles and I look for Benkei. He is not in it. The war tales name him in passing, nothing more. I think that matters. The legend places him at his master's side in every battle. The record does not.

scenes.narration: Then comes the winter of 1185. Yoritomo turns on his brother, and Yoshitsune has to run. I read that he leaves by ship, the sea rises, the vessels break up, and the party scatters. A short list of followers survives, and among them I find the monk once more, now with a name and a title: Musashibo Benkei. Then the trail goes cold. For more than a year Yoshitsune hides in temples and mountains, until in 1187 he reaches Hiraizumi in the north, under the protection of Fujiwara no Hidehira. The legend says the monk never leaves his side.

scenes.narration: Here is the story I most want to check. The Noh play Ataka, written some three centuries later, sends them north in disguise, as travelling mountain priests, to a barrier gate. The guard demands to see the scroll of their temple fund. The monk has none, so he unrolls a blank scroll and reads as if it were full. He even strikes his own master with a staff, to fool the guard. The older Gikeiki sets that beating at a river ferry, with a fan. I have no record of any of it. I put a question mark beside it.

scenes.narration: Back on the riverbank, the same day. I tell an old groom from the nearby stables that I am a travelling merchant. He watches the hill as he talks. The monk, he says, sits up every night with his prayer beads while his master sleeps. He eats little and says less. The men call him the quiet one. I ask whether he really once dragged a temple bell up a mountain. The groom laughs, and says he has only ever seen the man lift a bucket for the horses. I did not expect that. I write it down.

scenes.narration: Now to why they are here. In 1187 Hidehira dies, the lord who sheltered Yoshitsune. His dying wish, a Kyoto courtier writes, is that his sons serve Yoshitsune as their general. His son Yasuhira inherits, and Yoritomo's letters begin to arrive, demanding the fugitive. I read that Kamakura threatens to march on the north unless he is handed over. Yasuhira weighs his father's last wish against his own survival. I think he is a frightened man doing arithmetic. By the early summer of 1189, the arithmetic is done.

scenes.narration: Now I try to find the monk. The Gikeiki says Benkei plants himself before the hall and holds the door while his master meets his end inside. Arrows strike him until he looks like a man wearing a straw rain cape. He does not fall. The riders hang back, thinking him alive, until a horse brushes past and he topples. I stare through the smoke, and I cannot see a doorway, or a monk. Only dust. I write that down too. An honest reporter admits when the best story is out of sight.

scenes.narration: Another page, and the monk gets no entry of his own at all. The Gikeiki, written long after, makes him grow. By the age of the Noh plays, he is the quiet strength behind the doomed prince. In 1840 the kabuki stage turns that play into Kanjincho, still one of its best-loved scenes. I think Japan did not invent him from nothing. It took a name and a title, and gave it the one thing a chronicle rarely offers: a face, a voice, and a loyalty with no limit.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Back in my own century, I climb Takadachi hill, now a quiet grassy ridge above the river in Hiraizumi. In 1689 the poet Matsuo Basho stood near here and wrote that the summer grass is all that remains of warriors' dreams. He wept. I think it is the most honest sentence ever written about this place. A small hall on the summit holds a wooden statue of Yoshitsune. The monk gets no statue of his own up here, just grass.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Japan still uses the monk in everyday speech. When a line of lorries is stuck in a blizzard, unable to go forward or back, the news calls it tachi-ojo, a standing death, a word many say was born from the monk on his hill. Another phrase names a man's shin as Benkei's crying place, because even Benkei, the saying goes, would weep if struck there. I think this is the real measure of a legend. Nobody needs a record for a monk who has become a word for a snowstorm and a bruise.
